query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Directional solidification with a finely tuned cooling rate that refines the lamellar spacing to the submicron scale will simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting a two-phase lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with typical micron-scale lamellar spacing.
generation.intervention: Implement a directional solidification process with a precisely controlled, high cooling rate to achieve a submicron lamellar structure during casting.
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical loading conditions representative of structural applications; the alloy composition and processing parameters are maintained such that the two-phase eutectic fcc/B2 structure is preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in lamellar spacing to the submicron scale, leading to an increased density of coherent phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The refined lamellar structure acts as a more effective barrier to dislocation motion (thus enhancing strength) while providing more uniformly distributed and coherent interfaces that facilitate plastic deformation (thereby enhancing ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: An approximate improvement of around 10–20% in both yield strength and fracture strain relative to conventionally cast (micron-scale lamellar) EHEAs.
generation.baseline: EHEA produced by conventional casting methods, resulting in typically micron-scale lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with established strength and ductility levels.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected only for eutectic HEAs maintaining the two-phase fcc/B2 structure; deviations in composition or processing that alter phase stability or lead to segregation might not yield the predicted performance improvements. The mechanical benefits are anticipated under standard structural loading at ambient or mildly elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: While the refined microstructure is predicted to improve both properties, the precise magnitude of the enhancements depends on the exact cooling rate and resultant lamellar dimensions, which require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same eutectic high-entropy alloy: one using conventional casting to obtain the standard micron-scale lamellar structure and the other using directional solidification with a controlled cooling rate to achieve submicron lamellar spacing. Characterize the microstructure via electron microscopy and conduct standardized tensile tests at room temperature to measure strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directional solidified specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (≥10% increase) in both yield strength and fracture strain compared to the conventionally cast specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: Research on eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) for structural applications first demonstrated that as-cast lamellar fcc/B2 microstructures could deliver a promising balance of strength and ductility in AlCoCrFeNi EHEAs (PMC4145285). Cold rolling was then shown to increase the alloy’s strength but severely reduced ductility. Attempts to transform or refine the as-cast lamellae by minor post-processing and modest cold work improved strength but sacrificed ductility, underscoring the challenge of achieving a harmonious combination of both properties in EHEAs.
decision.unsolved: A single-step technique to refine or rearrange the as-cast eutectic lamellar structure so that both strength and ductility are enhanced simultaneously remains elusive. While modest deformation or heat treatment can raise strength, ductility typically drops, indicating the need for a more systematic control of lamellar spacing and interface characteristics without resorting to complex composition changes.
decision.lever: Directional solidification with a tuned solidification rate to achieve a submicron lamellar structure in the as-cast EHEA, preserving the two-phase eutectic nature while reducing lamellar spacing for enhanced obstacle strengthening and improved interfacial plastic compatibility.
decision.why: Refining lamellar spacing during solidification increases the barrier to dislocation motion (improving strength) while maintaining or even improving the ability for plastic flow if the interfaces are coherent and well-distributed. This approach directly addresses the trade-off between strength and ductility, attaches to the as-cast nature of the material, and does not rely upon additional alloying elements.
